Q: Split integer into chunks to monitor workflow A:

You don't need complex libraries for this. A simple generator or list comprehension with a step in range is the cleanest way to handle row chunks.

Python

def get_chunks(data, n):
    for i in range(0, len(data), n):
        yield data[i:i + n]

# Usage with gspread rows
rows = worksheet.get_all_values()
for chunk in get_chunks(rows, 100):
    print(f"Processing {len(chunk)} rows...")
    # Your logic here

This keeps your memory usage low and your logic straightforward

Q: Why does recursion in scheme macro cause error A:

If I may take the liberty of assuming that you don't actually care about factorial and are more interested in learning about recursive macros, then or is a classic example.

(define-syntax or
  (syntax-rules ()
    [(_) #f]
    [(_ e) e]
    [(_ e1 e2 e3 ...)
     (let ([t e1]) (if t t (or e2 e3 ...)))]))

Incremental expansion example:

;; Original
(or (f x) (g y z) "error")

;; First expansion
(let ([t (f x)])
  (if t
      t
      (or (g y z) "error")))

;; Second expansion
(let ([t (f x)])
  (if t
      t
      (let ([t (g y z)])
        (if t
            t
            (or "error")))))

;; Third expansion
(let ([t (f x)])
  (if t
      t
      (let ([t (g y z)])
        (if t
            t
            "error"))))

The or macro makes for a more realistic example because the recursive process operates on the syntactic structure -- a list of arbitrary expressions -- whereas fact requires a single, highly specific argument -- a positive integer literal -- and doesn't have any real work to do besides unwrapping the argument and handing it off to the factorial procedure.

Q: Required/Aria-required for a form where all fields but one are required A:

Non-compliance with "Labels or Instructions"

Yes, it is a concrete accessibility violation at Level A, specified under "Success Criterion 3.3.2: Labels or Instructions".
Direct link to the relevant content:
https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/labels-or-instructions#benefits

ARIA is not a visual fix

Secondly, any ARIA solution is for the screen reader users. Sighted users have no interaction with ARIA attributes and accessibility is not solely about screen reader users. Therefore, lack of visible instructions cannot be remediated by adding invisible instructions.

The Logical Fallacy of the "Optional" Indicator

Everything is required so why add those indicators?

  • If there are optional fields, then by definition not everything is required.
  • Are users supposed to deduce that fields not indicated as "optional" should be "required"? To make this deduction, one should first arrive at an optional field, right?
  • Web forms are not intended to add cognitive loads to users. In practice, many users may realise they missed some required fields, after having submitted the form.
  • Moreover, accidentally filling in an optional field will not generate an error, when the form is submitted. How meaningful is it to indicate the only fields that will never generate errors, filled in or not?

A message will help

As already suggested, a message could be added saying "all fields except...". That would technically prevent the concrete failure, if it is implemented properly.
However, even this solution relies on a user's working memory. (WCAG 2.1 is introduced to especially address the issues the users with cognitive disabilities encounter.)

Asterisks are just announced as "star" and they do not always mean "required"

Please also keep in mind that adding asterisks alone would also be another failure, unless there is an explanatory text that reads what an asterisk denotes. They will have to be hidden from the screen reader users. Furthermore, it is an assumption that all users see asterisks as required fields' indicators.

The best and the easiest solution

Add text that reads "required" for all required fields.

Useful Links showing how:

WCAG
https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/html/H90
Government of Canada
https://wet-boew.github.io/v4.0-ci/demos/formvalid/formvalid-en.html
Deque University
https://dequeuniversity.com/tips/identify-required-elements

Q: Mixing GCC/LLVM C2y preprocessor vector extension with arrays and alternatives for LLVM __builtin_vectorelements in GCC A:

Short answer: there’s no direct GCC equivalent to __builtin_vectorelements.

Use sizeof(vec) / sizeof(vec[0]) for element count, or wrap it in a macro. For generic handling, combine _Generic + sizeof or rely on GCC vector extensions (__attribute__((vector_size))) and compute length manually.

Q: PostgreSQL 9.3: How to insert upper case UUID into table A:

tl;dr

UUIDs are 128-bit values, not text. The hex text you see is for human consumption, not computers.

In years past, the hexadecimal representation of a UUID was required to be all-lowercase. But no longer. You may see the hex text of a UUID in all-lowercase, all-UPPERCASE, or in mIxEDcaSe.

👉🏽 If you want a particular case (lower or upper), from any system (Postgres or otherwise), be sure to convert the hex text yourself. Never assume.

UUID is not text

You have misunderstood the essence of a UUID. A UUID is not text. A UUID is not composed of characters.

128 bits

A UUID is composed of 128 bits. Nothing more, nothing less.

Some of those bits have certain meaning. The meaning varies by which Version of UUID.

Hexadecimal representation

Humans do not do well when reading or writing one hundred and twenty eight 1 and 0 characters.

So when communicating with humans, we use a canonical representation where the 128 bits are converted into 32 hexadecimal digits. The hex digits (0-9, a-f/A-F) are grouped with hyphen characters as a delimiter, for a total of 36 characters.

For example:

019dcb4d-bd9f-7180-96ac-b54e8ad92e39

Native UUID in Postgres

Postgres has for decades supported UUID as a native data type. This means UUID values are stored as 128 bits. Postgres does not store hex characters. Postgres does not store text for a UUID column.

When you retrieve a UUID value for display on the console, the value is converted to hexadecimal characters rather sending 128 0 & 1 characters.

UUID specification

UUIDs have been formally defined in a written specification for decades. This is a large part of the success of UUIDs across the industry.

The two most recent specs have been managed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The earlier one, RFC 4122, was obsoleted by RFC 9562 in 2024.

The previous spec required the hexadecimal representation to be in lowercase, while also requiring implementations to parse UPPERCASE inputs.

Unfortunately, many popular implementations violated this requirement. At one point, Microsoft even released an implementation with miXEdCaSE (good grief!).

So in the current spec, RFC 9562, the authors abandoned that all-lowercase requirement. Any case is allowed for input and for output of hexadecimal representation.

By the way, RFC 9562 introduces two new UUID Versions, Version 6 and Version 7. Both are optimized for efficient indexing in a database to yield better performance. Postgres 18+ offers a built-in function to generate Version 7 UUID values.

Solution

You may receive the hex text representing a UUID value in any case. So, if you care about the case, manage it yourself. See the correct Answer by RPA Consultant, and the Answer by Renzo.

Postgres

You can manage the case in Postgres, using the built-in lower and upper string functions.

lower ( id_ :: text )

upper ( id_ :: text )

Programming language

You may choose to handle the case in the programming language of your app.

For example, in Java use methods on the String class:

UUID id = myResultSet.getObject( "id_" , UUID.class );  // Retrieve from UUID column in Postgres database.
String uuidText = id.toString().toLowerCase(); 

String uuidText = id.toString().toUpperCase();
